newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq denies U.S. attack, sees U.S. election ploy.
newsitem.headline: Iraq denies U.S. attack, sees U.S. election ploy.

text.p: The United States said on Sunday a U.S. jet had fired a missile at an Iraqi radar, but Baghdad denied the incident and accused the White House of spreading "false news" to help President Bill Clinton's re-election chances.
The White House said a U.S. Air Force F-16 jet enforcing a no-fly zone in southern Iraq on Saturday was targeted by Iraqi radar and fired on the Iraqi installation in response.
"Such American allegations are baseless. No incident of any kind has occurred in Iraq's air space," said the official Iraqi News Agency, quoting an Iraqi Foreign Ministry spokesman.
"Fabricating this false news is part of the U.S. election campaign, the U.S. style," INA quoted him as saying.

White House spokesman Barry Toiv said the pilot of the F-16 believed he had been illuminated by the missile-tracking radar of the mobile surface-to-air missile battery, a hostile act that allows U.S. pilots to fire missiles in retaliation.
The pilot fired a single High-speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM) at what he believed was a mobile surface-to-air missile battery. The plane later returned safely to its base in Saudi Arabia.

The Washington Times, which originally reported the incident, said there was some question about whether the pilot was actually illuminated by the Iraqi air defence battery, and the U.S. Central Command was investigating the incident.
The spokesman said Iraq was still committed to a decision not to fire at U.S. and allied jets patrolling two no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.
The decision was taken in September after a confrontation with the United States because of Baghdad's backing of a Kurdish group in its north against a rival faction.
The United States responded by attacking southern Iraq with missiles and extending a southern no-fly zone for Iraqi planes from the 32nd to the 33rd parallel.
Iraq initially countered the U.S. move by vowing to shoot down Western allied planes patrolling the zones but then decided to refrain from such attacks.

"Iraq is still committed to its decision, which gives apportunity for political action as a response to a proposal by friendly countries, particularly Russia and France, to handle the illegal and illegitimate two no-fly zones," the spokesman said.

Baghdad has said many times that it does not recognise the zones, imposed after the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait to protect Kurds in the north and dissident Shi'ite Moslems in southern marshlands against attack by Iraqi forces.
